mainEntity.name: What's the difference between simple and compound interest?

acceptedAnswer.text: Simple interest is calculated only on the original principal. Compound interest is calculated on the principal plus any interest already earned, so it grows faster over time.

mainEntity.name: How often should interest compound for the best results?

acceptedAnswer.text: More frequent compounding (daily or monthly) produces slightly higher returns than annual compounding at the same nominal rate, though the difference is usually small.

mainEntity.name: Should I enter my bank's APY or interest rate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Enter the interest rate before compounding. If only an APY is listed, enter it as the rate with annual compounding so compounding isn't counted twice.

mainEntity.name: What's a realistic compound growth rate to assume?

acceptedAnswer.text: Historical long-term stock market averages run around 7-10% before inflation, though returns vary significantly year to year and aren't guaranteed. Savings accounts pay a variable rate that follows central-bank rates.

mainEntity.name: Does this calculator account for inflation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, optionally. With Adjust for Inflation on, the Real Purchasing Power figure divides the final balance by (1 + inflation)years to show its value in today's money.
Less than most people think. At 5% for 10 years, $10,000 grows to $16,289 compounded annually, $16,470 monthly and $16,487 daily — the rate and time invested matter far more.
A quick mental shortcut: divide 72 by your annual growth rate to estimate how many years it takes an investment to double. At 8% growth, that's about 9 years.
